stem: A 58-year-old man who has smoked 2 packs per day for 30 years is diagnosed with lung cancer. He says he wants to quit but cannot, and that his first cigarette each morning gives an intense feeling of pleasure.
oneliner: 58M + 2 packs/day for 30 y + newly diagnosed lung cancer + cannot quit + intense pleasure from first cigarette → reward mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains the reinforcing effect of smoking?

options.A: Activation of opioid receptors in the periaqueductal gray
options.C: Stimulation of VTA neurons increasing dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens
options.E: Potentiation of GABA-A receptors in the cortex

whyNot.A: That mediates **analgesia and opioid reward**, not nicotine
whyNot.B: Would be **sedating or appetite-related**, not a euphoric reward
whyNot.D: Relates to **anxiety and fear learning**, not reward
whyNot.E: That is the action of **benzodiazepines and alcohol**

answer: Nicotine increases dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic reward pathway)
why: Nicotine binds **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** on **ventral tegmental area (VTA)** neurons, which fire more and release **dopamine into the nucleus accumbens**. This **reward circuit** reinforces use and drives dependence.

idea.rule: Addictive drugs share dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens.
also: Opioids inhibit GABA neurons in the VTA

stem: A 56-year-old man is hospitalized for a hip fracture repair. He drinks a pint of whiskey daily but has not told the staff. On hospital day 3 he is agitated and tremulous. Temperature is 38.2 C, pulse 128/min, and blood pressure 168/96 mm Hg. He is drenched in sweat and says insects are crawling on the walls. He is disoriented to place and time. He has no rigidity or clonus and takes no new drugs.
oneliner: 56M + daily whiskey, hip fracture + hospital day 3 + agitation, tremor, T 38.2, HR 128, BP 168/96 + sweating + visual hallucinations + disoriented + no rigidity or clonus → neurochemical change?
ask: Which change best explains his condition?

options.D: Loss of enhanced GABA inhibition with unopposed glutamate excitation

whyNot.A: **Serotonin syndrome**: clonus and hyperreflexia, with a serotonergic drug; none here
whyNot.B: **Anticholinergic**: dry flushed skin and dilated pupils, not drenching sweat
whyNot.C: **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome**: lead-pipe rigidity and an antipsychotic; none here
whyNot.E: **Opioid withdrawal**: yawning, piloerection, diarrhea; clear sensorium

answer: Alcohol withdrawal: reduced GABA-A inhibition and glutamate (NMDA) rebound
why: Chronic alcohol **enhances GABA-A inhibition and blunts NMDA glutamate**. When intake stops, **inhibition falls and excitation rebounds**: **autonomic hyperactivity** (tachycardia, sweating, fever) and **visual hallucinations** with disorientation = **delirium tremens**.
chain: Chronic alcohol boosts GABA, blunts glutamate

idea.rule: Withdrawal is the rebound of whatever the drug was suppressing (GABA tone down, glutamate up).
also: Benzodiazepine and barbiturate withdrawal: same GABA rebound, seizures
Opioid withdrawal: noradrenergic rebound (yawning, diarrhea, piloerection)
Treat alcohol withdrawal with a benzodiazepine (replace the lost GABA effect)

stem: A 40-year-old woman has been separated from her husband, changed jobs, and moved house within the past 4 months. She feels anxious and sleeps poorly. Physical examination is normal.
oneliner: 40F + separation, job change, move in 4 months + anxiety, poor sleep + normal exam → expected finding?
ask: Which laboratory finding is most likely?

whyNot.C: No link to stress; **no hypercalcemia** features
whyNot.E: Not produced by **psychological stress** and no blood loss or chronic disease

why: Chronic stress activates the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis**. High **cortisol** and catecholamines **suppress lymphocyte proliferation and cytokine release**.
